title: KUMA: Koopman Separation and Multilevel Extraction for Time Series
one_liner: Split the hidden flow in time series into two simple pieces, then use a smart tower of filters to pick the right tokens for each level.
lead: Time series (like stock prices or sensor readings) are messy: they have changing patterns over time, too many numbers to process efficiently, and lots of wasted information. KUMA untangles this by splitting the flow into two kinds of change — one smooth and predictable (the Koopman part) and one grainy and random (the leftover) — then builds a tower of filters to pick which numbers actually matter at each layer.

problem.h2: Three traps in time series forecasting
paras: Today's time series forecasters face three hard problems. First, they choke on computational cost: the longer the history and the more dimensions (like tracking ten sensors at once), the heavier the math becomes. Second, the tokens (the individual numbers in the series) are not equally useful: some carry real signal, others are just noise or repeat what you already know. Third, the pattern itself shifts over time — yesterday's drift is not today's drift, so a model trained on old data stumbles when the world changes.

A beginner might try to just throw more layers at it: use a bigger model, feed in more history, hope the learning figures it out. This breaks because (1) the cost explodes, (2) the model drowns in garbage tokens, and (3) non-stationary dynamics (when the rules change mid-series) confuse the model into learning brittle patterns that don't generalize.

callout.b: The core idea in one sentence.
callout.html: Separate the series into two parts: a smooth predictable flow and a grainy residual, then build a multi-layer tower that picks the right numbers for each layer and focuses on the ones that matter.

steps.text: Feed the multivariate time series with all its noise and non-stationary shifts.
The module learns, for this specific input, which part is smooth Koopman flow and which is grainy residual.
Embed the separated series into tokens (numbers) at the base of the tower.
UMA applies element-wise scores and linear attention: each layer drops low-value tokens and keeps high-value ones.
The top of the tower reads only the selected tokens and forecasts the future.

paras: KUMA changes which tokens survive the journey from input to output. It does not invent new tokens or change how tokens are learned — instead, it builds an input-dependent gate: the Koopman module learns, for the current series, which dimensions carry true pattern and which are noise, then the UMA tower explicitly drops redundant tokens at each layer.

hidden.name: Token importance: which tokens actually matter for this forecast
paras: KUMA measures an invisible quantity: how much does each token contribute to the final forecast? Some tokens are signal, some are noise, and some are repetitive. A token with high importance means the series cannot predict the future without it. A low-importance token is either garbage or redundant with other tokens.

The paper estimates this via two routes. First, the Koopman module infers which dimensions contain true dynamics (Koopman part) versus leftover (residual) — this gives an input-dependent importance mask. Second, the UMA tower applies element-wise scoring (a learned number between 0 and 1 for each number, which works quickly because it is independent: each number gets one score, no pairing) and linear scoring (which measures influence using simpler math than full cross-pairing, so it runs faster as the layer grows). The higher the score, the more that number influences the forecast.

heat.caption: Darker tokens: high importance for the forecast. Light tokens: redundant or noise. KUMA learns to drop the light ones.

reads.html: Imagine you are reading a 100-page report to predict tomorrow's weather. Some pages carry vital weather data; some are just noise from the printer; some repeat information you already have. Token importance is the score that says 'this page matters' or 'this page is junk.' KUMA learns to drop the junk.

In the Koopman decomposition, the input-dependent operator learns which modes (the frequencies and patterns hidden in the data) are truly Koopman-stable versus residual-volatile. UMA then applies scoring weights (numbers in the range 0 to 1) to each number; numbers with low weights contribute little to the forecast's direction and can be dropped or downsampled without harming the result.

mechanism.h2: How Koopman separation and multilevel filtering work together
paras: Here is the causal chain. Time series are often non-stationary (the rules change), so a single fixed model struggles. KUMA splits the problem: the Koopman module learns a decomposition specific to the current input, separating slow, smooth, predictable change (Koopman dynamics) from fast, grainy, unpredictable residuals. This split is learned, not hand-coded — it adapts to the data.

Once split, the UMA tower builds a sequence of layers (encoder side) that progressively filter numbers. At the bottom, all numbers arrive; at each layer, element-wise scoring (a learned score for each number) selects which ones pass upward. Additionally, linear scoring (a simpler way to compute importance that avoids slowing down as layer size grows) scores which sequences within each layer matter most without recalculating everything. The result: redundant and noisy numbers drop out, leaving only the signal. This two-pronged approach — splitting the series to reduce non-stationary confusion, and filtering numbers to kill redundancy — cuts computational cost because fewer numbers flow through higher layers, while preserving the true patterns because the filters learned what matters.

Why this works: by separating Koopman-stable from residual-volatile parts, the model sees a cleaner signal, so non-stationarity (when the pattern's rules shift over time) worries it less because the stable part remains stable. By filtering numbers multilevel, the model avoids computing expensive pair-wise scores over all numbers at every layer — it only focuses on the ones that passed the filter, which means fewer pairs to score at higher layers, so the time and memory shrink. The net effect is lower computational cost (fewer expensive operations), better number usage (only the useful ones stay), and more reliable forecasts because the model learns from pure signal without drowning in noise — when training sees only the true patterns without garbage, it converges to a simpler rule that generalizes better.

stages.s: Raw time series with noise and shifting patterns
Koopman module learns decomposition for this input
UMA base layer: encode all tokens
Filter layers: drop low-importance tokens at each level
Top layer reads only important tokens, forecasts future

math.words: The Koopman module splits the series into two parts. UMA then applies element-wise attention weights to each token and downsamples high-layer tokens by score. The overall loss combines forecast error with a small penalty on the importance scores to encourage sparsity.
math.equation: x_t = K(x_t) + R(x_t); y_pred = Decoder( UMA( Encoder(K, R) ) ); loss = MSE(y_pred, y_true) + lambda * sum_i (1 - a_i)^2
symbols: the input time series at step t
the Koopman part: smooth, predictable dynamics for this input
the residual part: grainy, hard-to-predict leftover
the attention weight (between 0 and 1) for token i
a small number controlling how aggressively we drop tokens
the forecast error: how far off the prediction is

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Input series has 10 tokens initially. Koopman identifies 8 as Koopman-stable, 2 as residual-volatile.
Layer 1 keeps tokens with score > 0.5: 7 tokens remain, 3 dropped. Cost saved = ~30% of base attention cost.
Layer 2: keeps top 4 most important tokens from the 7. Final layer forecasts using only 4 tokens.
Forecast error: 0.18 (same accuracy as keeping all 10), but 60% faster compute.

math.note: The decomposition into K and R makes the series less non-stationary (smoother), so attention and linear layers see clearer patterns. Token dropout via attention weights makes each layer leaner.

charts.title: Old approach (all tokens, all steps)
charts.note: Full attention over all tokens at all layers. Accurate but slow and wastes computation on noise.

charts.title: KUMA with Koopman + UMA filtering
charts.note: Koopman cleanses the input (so the model sees less noise and less pattern-shift), UMA filters numbers at each layer (so high layers pay attention only to the few that matter, not all of them). This reduces expensive cross-pair scoring: accuracy improves because the signal is clearer, and speed improves because fewer pairs need scoring.

items.b: Decomposition fails if the series is truly random.
items.html: If the series has no Koopman-stable structure (all residual), the decomposition learns nothing, and UMA has no strong tokens to keep. KUMA degrades to a standard model.
If the lambda penalty on importance scores is too high, UMA filters away tokens that look low-value in isolation but contain long-range dependencies. The forecast breaks.
The Koopman decomposition is learned fresh for each input, which is good; but if the non-stationarity is extreme (the rules change mid-batch), even the smooth part can shift, and forecasts suffer.

items.b: Done right: tune lambda, validate on held-out non-stationary windows.
items.html: Use cross-validation to find lambda that drops junk but keeps signal. Test on data where the pattern shifts mid-series to ensure the decomposition adapts.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a minimal version: (1) Take a real multivariate time series with known non-stationarity (e.g., energy consumption that changes seasonally, or a financial series with regime shifts). (2) Train a baseline model (a standard sequence model on all numbers) and measure forecast error, numbers per step, and wall-clock time. (3) Implement the Koopman decomposition as a trainable linear layer that learns to separate smooth and residual parts. (4) Add UMA as a simple two-layer tower: bottom keeps all numbers, top keeps the top-50% by importance score. (5) Compare: does the KUMA version forecast as well or better because the decomposition removes non-stationary noise, and does it run faster because filtering numbers reduces the pairs that need scoring?
demo.metric_eq: improvement = (baseline_error - kuma_error) / baseline_error; speedup = baseline_time / kuma_time; token_efficiency = (baseline_tokens - kuma_tokens) / baseline_tokens
demo.closing: The demo should make it impossible to miss that separating the series into stable and residual parts, combined with token filtering, reduces computational cost without sacrificing forecast accuracy — and sometimes even improves accuracy because the model is less confused by non-stationary noise.
